lead: A battery turns a chemical redox reaction into electrical energy. Primary batteries are used once and discarded; secondary batteries can be recharged by reversing the reaction. Performance is not one number: voltage, capacity, energy density, power density, self-discharge and cycle life decide whether a battery suits a remote, a phone, a UPS or an electric vehicle. This chapter classifies batteries, defines the standard parameters with units, and shows how to convert ampere-hours to watt-hours without mixing charge and energy.
prereq: You need: cell EMF, half-reactions and electrode potentials from 4.1; the Nernst equation from 4.2 explains why voltage falls as reactants are used.

blocks.text: An electrochemical cell produces electrical work from a spontaneous redox reaction. A battery is one or more cells connected in series or parallel, with terminals and packaging. In series, cell voltages add and capacity stays the same. In parallel, capacity adds and voltage stays the same.

A primary battery is made for one discharge. Its active materials are sealed, and the products are hard to convert back. Common examples are the zinc-carbon dry cell, the alkaline cell and the button cell in a watch. A secondary battery is rechargeable. Current in the reverse direction restores the active materials. Lead-acid, nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd) and lithium-ion are the main secondary types. Construction of lead-acid and Li-ion cells is in 4.6.
A practical battery must meet several requirements at once:

items: High energy density, so the battery is light and small for the energy it stores.
Stable voltage during discharge, so the device works as the battery drains.
Low internal resistance, so it can supply a large current without a big voltage drop.
Long cycle life for secondary cells, safety under abuse, low cost and low self-discharge during storage.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this energy systems or battery technology.

The open-circuit voltage of a cell is its EMF, set by the electrode potentials. Under load, the terminal voltage is lower: V<sub>terminal</sub> = EMF − I r, where I is current in amperes (A) and r is internal resistance in ohms (Ω). Nominal voltage is the label value, such as 1.5 V for a dry cell, 1.2 V for Ni-Cd, 3.7 V for a Li-ion cell, or 12 V for a lead-acid pack.

blocks.where: Q is charge in ampere-hours (Ah); I is current in amperes (A); t is time in hours (h).
E is energy in watt-hours (Wh); Q is charge in Ah; V is voltage in volts (V).

C-rate is the discharge rate in h⁻¹; I is current in A; Q<sub>rated</sub> is rated capacity in Ah. 1C means the full capacity is delivered in 1 h. DoD = (Q<sub>used</sub> ÷ Q<sub>rated</sub>) × 100%, where Q<sub>used</sub> is charge taken out in Ah. Coulombic efficiency = (Q<sub>discharge</sub> ÷ Q<sub>charge</sub>) × 100%, where both charges are in Ah.

Unit
What it tells you

Current as a multiple of rated capacity

blocks.text: Self-discharge is the charge lost per month while idle. Cycle life is the number of charge–discharge cycles before capacity falls to a stated fraction, often 80%. Power density in W kg⁻¹ measures how fast energy can be delivered. Energy density in Wh kg⁻¹ or Wh L⁻¹ measures stored energy per kilogram or per litre.
Wh kg⁻¹ is also called specific energy, and some books use energy density only for Wh L⁻¹; here we say which unit we mean.
A label such as 12 V, 100 Ah does not mean 100 Ah of energy. It means 100 Ah of charge at about 12 V. Convert to watt-hours first. Then compare chemistries by energy density and by power density.

items: Write the rated voltage V and rated capacity Q<sub>rated</sub> in Ah.
Find stored energy E = Q<sub>rated</sub> × V in Wh. Divide by 1000 for kWh.
For a load current I, find C-rate = I ÷ Q<sub>rated</sub> and ideal time t = Q<sub>rated</sub> ÷ I.
Find charge used Q<sub>used</sub> = I × t and depth of discharge DoD = Q<sub>used</sub> ÷ Q<sub>rated</sub> × 100%.
Check cycle life, self-discharge and the allowed DoD for the chemistry before choosing the battery.

blocks.text: A lead-acid battery used in an inverter is cheap and gives high current, but it is heavy and should not be deep-discharged often. A Li-ion phone battery stores more energy per kilogram but needs a protection circuit. The same Ah rating can therefore mean very different stored energy.

figure.caption: Battery classification: primary cells are single-use; secondary cells can be recharged. The two branches are the first check when a question asks for a suitable battery.

spec.aria: A battery classification tree splits into primary cells such as dry and alkaline cells and secondary cells such as lead-acid, lithium-ion and nickel-cadmium.

examples.question: A 12 V, 100 Ah lead-acid battery is discharged at a constant 5 A for 10 h. (a) Find its stored energy in Wh and kWh. (b) Find the charge used in Ah. (c) Find the depth of discharge. (d) Find the C-rate of the discharge.
steps: Rated voltage V = 12 V; rated capacity Q<sub>rated</sub> = 100 Ah.
Stored energy E = Q<sub>rated</sub> × V = 100 Ah × 12 V = 1200 Wh.
Charge used Q<sub>used</sub> = I × t = 5 A × 10 h = 50 Ah.
Depth of discharge DoD = (Q<sub>used</sub> ÷ Q<sub>rated</sub>) × 100% = (50 Ah ÷ 100 Ah) × 100% = 50%.
C-rate = I ÷ Q<sub>rated</sub> = 5 A ÷ 100 Ah = 0.05 h⁻¹, written 0.05C. This is a slow 20 h discharge.
examples.answer: The battery stores 1200 Wh (1.2 kWh); it uses 50 Ah, reaches 50% depth of discharge, and runs at 0.05C.
examples.check:
def main():
    V = 12.0
    Q = 100.0
    I = 5.0
    t = 10.0
    E_wh = V * Q
    E_kwh = E_wh / 1000.0
    Q_used = I * t
    dod = (Q_used / Q) * 100.0
    c_rate = I / Q
    print('{:g}'.format(E_wh))
    print('{:g}'.format(E_kwh))
    print('{:g}'.format(Q_used))
    print('{:g}'.format(dod))
    print('{:g}'.format(c_rate))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

traps: Ah is charge, not energy. A 12 V 100 Ah battery stores 1200 Wh; a 6 V 100 Ah battery stores 600 Wh. Convert with E = Q × V before comparing.
Nominal voltage is not the same as EMF or terminal voltage. Under load, V<sub>terminal</sub> = EMF − I r, so a 12 V battery may read 11 V while cranking a motor.
1C does not mean one coulomb. It means a current equal to the rated Ah value; 0.05C on 100 Ah is 5 A, which takes about 20 h.
Depth of discharge is not state of charge. 50% DoD means 50% used; 50% state of charge means 50% remains.
Primary does not mean low capacity, and secondary does not mean unlimited cycles. Button cells are primary; lead-acid is secondary but has limited cycle life.

quiz.q: Define a primary battery and a secondary battery. Give one example of each.
quiz.a: A primary battery is made for one discharge and is not recharged; example: dry cell or alkaline cell. A secondary battery is rechargeable; example: lead-acid, Ni-Cd or Li-ion.

quiz.q: Why is an Ah rating alone not enough to compare two batteries?
quiz.a: Ah is charge. Energy depends on charge and voltage through E = Q × V. A 12 V 100 Ah battery stores 1200 Wh, while a 6 V 100 Ah battery stores only 600 Wh. Compare Wh or Wh kg⁻¹.

quiz.q: A 6 V, 4.5 Ah battery supplies 1.5 A. Find its stored energy and its C-rate.
quiz.a: E = 6 V × 4.5 Ah = 27 Wh. C-rate = 1.5 A ÷ 4.5 Ah = 0.33 h⁻¹, that is 0.33C.

quiz.q: A 12 V, 50 Ah battery delivers 2 A for 10 h. Find the charge used and the depth of discharge.
quiz.a: Q<sub>used</sub> = 2 A × 10 h = 20 Ah. DoD = (20 Ah ÷ 50 Ah) × 100% = 40%.

quiz.q: Why does the terminal voltage of a battery fall when a motor draws a large current?
quiz.a: The battery has internal resistance r. The drop is I r, so V<sub>terminal</sub> = EMF − I r. A large current I gives a larger drop. The motor now runs at a lower voltage, so its speed falls. The current it draws depends on the mechanical load and rises sharply only if the motor is overloaded or stalled. Example: a car starter draws a very large current, and the I r drop pulls a 12 V battery down to about 11 V or less for a moment.

quiz.q: List four performance parameters of a battery with their units.
quiz.a: Any four: capacity in Ah; energy in Wh; energy density in Wh kg⁻¹; power density in W kg⁻¹; self-discharge in % per month; cycle life in cycles; C-rate in h⁻¹.

quiz.q: A phone battery is rated 3.7 V, 3000 mAh. Find its energy in Wh. If the phone draws 600 mA, find the C-rate and the ideal discharge time.
quiz.a: Q = 3000 mAh = 3.0 Ah. E = 3.7 V × 3.0 Ah = 11.1 Wh. C-rate = 0.6 A ÷ 3.0 Ah = 0.2 h⁻¹, that is 0.2C. Ideal time = 3.0 Ah ÷ 0.6 A = 5 h.

beyond: Not for the exam. Battery research now pushes lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion cells for grid storage, solid electrolytes for safety, and recycling of lithium, cobalt and nickel. Battery management systems estimate state of charge and state of health from voltage, current and temperature. Search next for C-rate testing, coulombic efficiency and sodium-ion chemistry.
